questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a transit fare hike is a movement along aggregate demand
questions.stem: Explain why raising transit fares changes the price level rather than shifting aggregate demand.

answer.exemplar: A fare hike changes the overall price level, so it is a movement along the aggregate demand curve rather than a shift of the curve itself; the quantity of real output demanded changes at each price level only when a non-price determinant changes.

questions.explanation: Aggregate demand shifts only when a non-price determinant like spending or money changes. A price change causes movement along the curve, not a shift of it.
questions.hint: Price changes move along, not shift.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the spending multiplier from a marginal propensity to consume
questions.stem: With a marginal propensity to consume of zero point eight, what is the spending multiplier for a transit project?
questions.explanation: The spending multiplier equals one divided by one minus the marginal propensity to consume, so one divided by zero point two equals five. A higher propensity to consume raises the multiplier.
questions.hint: Divide one by one minus mpc.

questions.stem: If consumption is fifty, investment is twenty, government spending is fifteen, and net exports are negative five, what is aggregate expenditure?
questions.explanation: Aggregate expenditure equals fifty plus twenty plus fifteen minus five, which is eighty million. All four components sum to total demand.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a price-level change as movement
questions.stem: A transit region report shows the price level rising while real output demanded falls.

options.text: A shift in aggregate supply only
options.misconception: attributes a demand response to supply

options.text: A rightward shift of aggregate demand
options.misconception: treats a price rise as a shift determinant

options.text: A leftward shift of aggregate demand
options.misconception: confuses higher prices with lower demand shift

options.text: A movement up along the aggregate demand curve

questions.explanation: A rising price level causes movement up along the aggregate demand curve. Shifts require non-price determinants to change.
questions.hint: Price changes move along the curve.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why lower rates stimulate investment
questions.stem: A board chart shows investment rising after the transit region's rates fall.

options.text: Investment is insensitive to rates in the short run
options.misconception: denies rate sensitivity of investment

options.text: Lower rates raise capital costs and cut investment
options.misconception: reverses the rate effect on capital cost

options.text: Lower rates reduce capital costs and raise investment
Lower rates shift supply, not demand
options.misconception: misplaces investment in supply

questions.explanation: Lower rates reduce the cost of capital, encouraging firms to invest more. This links monetary policy to aggregate demand.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why surpluses can be contractionary
questions.stem: Explain why a sustained budget surplus can be contractionary for the transit region.

answer.exemplar: A sustained surplus means government collects more than it spends, withdrawing net demand from the economy and shifting aggregate demand to the left.

questions.explanation: A surplus withdraws net demand from the economy, shifting aggregate demand left. Surpluses are contractionary.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the offset to stimulus from crowding out
questions.stem: If stimulus adds thirty million to demand but crowding out removes eight million, what is the net demand change?
questions.explanation: Net demand change equals thirty million minus eight million, or twenty two million. Crowding out offsets part of the stimulus.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of a higher reserve ratio on the multiplier
questions.stem: The transit region's central bank raises the reserve requirement from ten to twenty percent.

options.text: The money multiplier becomes zero
options.misconception: overstates the effect of a higher ratio

options.text: The money multiplier rises from ten to twenty
options.misconception: reverses the ratio effect on the multiplier

options.text: The money multiplier stays at ten
options.misconception: ignores the reserve ratio change

options.text: The money multiplier falls from ten to five

questions.explanation: Raising the reserve ratio from ten to twenty percent cuts the multiplier from ten to five. Higher requirements reduce money creation.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how foreign income affects net exports
questions.stem: A board report shows rising foreign income boosting exports from the transit region.

options.text: Higher foreign income lowers exports and net exports
options.misconception: reverses the foreign income effect

options.text: Higher foreign income raises exports and net exports
Foreign income does not affect domestic exports
options.misconception: ignores the foreign demand channel

options.text: Higher foreign income raises imports instead
options.misconception: confuses foreign income with domestic income

questions.explanation: Higher foreign income increases demand for domestic exports, raising net exports and shifting aggregate demand right. This is a demand shifter.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why policy lags matter for stabilization
questions.stem: Explain why recognition and implementation lags can make stabilization policy mistimed.

answer.exemplar: Recognition and implementation lags mean policy may take effect after conditions change, so stimulus can arrive during recovery and worsen inflation instead of easing recession.

questions.explanation: Lags can cause policy to hit at the wrong time, turning intended stimulus into overheating. Timing matters for stabilization.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the spending multiplier and compare
questions.stem: With an mpc of zero point nine, what is the spending multiplier for a transit grant?
questions.explanation: The spending multiplier is one over one minus zero point nine, or ten. A high mpc gives a large multiplier.
questions.hint: Divide one by one minus mpc.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the first step in monetary transmission
questions.stem: A transit board analyst describes the first step of monetary transmission.

options.text: Consumer spending jumps first
options.misconception: skips both rate and investment channels

options.text: Firms immediately raise investment
options.misconception: skips the rate channel

options.text: The central bank changes the money supply
The government changes tax rates
options.misconception: confuses monetary with fiscal policy

questions.explanation: Monetary transmission begins with a change in the money supply, which then affects rates, investment, and demand. Investment and spending respond later.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify when fiscal stimulus is most effective
questions.stem: A board report compares stimulus effectiveness in a deep recession versus a boom.

options.text: Stimulus is never effective in any phase
options.misconception: denies fiscal policy effectiveness

options.text: Stimulus is more effective in a boom with tight labor markets
options.misconception: ignores capacity constraints

options.text: Stimulus is equally effective in both phases
options.misconception: ignores the output gap size

options.text: Stimulus is more effective in a deep recession with slack

questions.explanation: Stimulus is more effective when slack exists, since resources are idle. In a boom it mainly raises prices.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why tax cuts are expansionary
questions.stem: Explain why a cut in transit payroll taxes is expansionary fiscal policy.

answer.exemplar: A payroll tax cut raises disposable income, which boosts consumption spending, a component of aggregate demand, shifting the curve to the right.

questions.explanation: Lower taxes raise disposable income and consumption, shifting aggregate demand right. This is expansionary fiscal policy.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why spending cuts are contractionary
questions.stem: If a board cuts spending by six million with an mpc of zero point five, by how much does output fall?
questions.explanation: The spending multiplier is two, so a six million cut reduces output by twelve million. Cuts contract demand by more than their size.
questions.hint: Multiply the cut by the multiplier.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a change in government spending as a shifter
questions.stem: The transit board increases its capital budget for new rail cars.

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts left due to higher government spending
options.misconception: reverses the spending effect on demand

options.text: Aggregate demand shifts right due to higher government spending
Only the price level changes, not demand
options.misconception: confuses a shifter with movement along

options.text: Aggregate supply shifts right instead
options.misconception: misplaces spending in supply

questions.explanation: Higher government spending is a non-price determinant that shifts aggregate demand right. It is not a price change or supply shift.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the multiplier exceeds one
questions.stem: A board analyst explains why the spending multiplier exceeds one.

options.text: The multiplier equals the tax rate
options.misconception: confuses multiplier with tax rate

options.text: Spending is fully saved in the first round
options.misconception: denies the respending channel

options.text: Each round of spending becomes income and is partly respent
Spending only affects prices, not output
options.misconception: ignores the output response

questions.explanation: The multiplier exceeds one because each round of spending becomes income and part is respent. Full saving would make it one.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the tax multiplier is smaller
questions.stem: Explain why the tax multiplier is smaller in absolute value than the spending multiplier.

answer.exemplar: A tax change first alters disposable income, and only the marginal propensity to consume portion is spent, so the first-round demand effect is smaller than direct spending.

questions.explanation: Only part of a tax change is spent, so the first-round effect is smaller than direct spending. This makes the tax multiplier smaller.
questions.hint: Only part of a tax change is spent.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bond purchases expand money supply
questions.stem: If the central bank buys ten million in bonds with a reserve ratio of twenty five percent, by how much does the money supply expand?
questions.explanation: The money multiplier is four, so a ten million purchase expands the money supply by forty million. Purchases add reserves to banks.
questions.hint: Multiply the purchase by the multiplier.
